title: Black Stool After Drinking: Harmless Cause or Bleeding?
excerpt: Black stool after drinking? Tarry, sticky black stool can mean bleeding and needs urgent care. Here's how to tell it apart from harmless causes like Pepto-Bismol, iron, or dark food, and when to go to the ER.
metaDescription: Black stool after drinking? Tarry black stool can mean GI bleeding and needs urgent care. How to tell it apart from Pepto-Bismol, iron, or dark food.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
> **Get emergency care now (read this first).** This article is general information, not medical advice, and it can't examine you. **Go to the emergency room or call 911 if** you have black, tarry stool together with dizziness, fainting, a racing heart, cold or clammy skin, shortness of breath, or confusion, or if you vomit blood or material that looks like coffee grounds. **Call your doctor the same day if** you have black stool you can't explain with Pepto-Bismol, iron, charcoal, or food; if it lasts more than two or three days after you stop those products; if you also have stomach pain that won't go away; or if you take blood thinners, aspirin, or ibuprofen-type painkillers regularly, have liver disease, or have had an ulcer before. If you're unsure, err on the side of being seen. A quick stool test can settle the question.

**The honest answer first:** black stool after drinking has two very different explanations, and you need to rule out the dangerous one first. Black, tarry, sticky, shiny, foul-smelling stool (doctors call it melena) can mean bleeding high in your digestive tract, and heavy drinking raises that risk. That is a medical emergency, especially with dizziness, weakness, a racing heart, or vomiting blood. The more common, harmless explanation is something you took or ate. Pepto-Bismol is the number one culprit: its active ingredient, bismuth, reacts with traces of sulfur in your gut and turns your stool (and sometimes your tongue) black for a day or two. Iron pills, activated charcoal, and very dark foods can do the same thing. This guide walks you through how to tell them apart and when you need to get checked.

**The quick rules:** If you took Pepto-Bismol, an iron supplement, or activated charcoal in the last day or two and you feel fine, black stool is expected and should clear up within a few days of stopping. If the stool is **tarry, sticky, shiny, and unusually foul-smelling**, if you **vomited blood or something that looks like coffee grounds**, or if you feel **dizzy, faint, weak, short of breath, or your heart is racing**, treat it as possible internal bleeding and get medical care the same day. If you're about to pass out or are vomiting blood, call 911.

## Why Black Stool Shows Up After a Night of Drinking

Normal stool is brown because of bile, a greenish-yellow fluid your liver makes to digest fat. As bile moves through your intestines, gut bacteria break it down into brown pigments. When something changes that process, or when something dark gets added to it, the color changes.

After a night out, a few things tend to happen at once:

- **You reach for remedies.** Pepto-Bismol for an upset stomach, an "activated charcoal" hangover product, or a multivitamin with iron are common morning-after choices. All three can turn stool black.
- **You ate or drank unusual things.** Dark beers, red wine, black licorice shots, dark-colored cocktails, blueberries, and late-night food with heavy dark coloring can all darken stool, sometimes to near-black.
- **Your gut is irritated.** Alcohol irritates the stomach lining. In most people that means a sore stomach or loose stools. In some people, especially those who drink heavily, take certain painkillers, or vomit hard and repeatedly, the irritation can lead to bleeding.

The first two are harmless. The third is the one worth understanding, because blood that enters the digestive tract high up (in the esophagus, stomach, or first part of the small intestine) gets partly digested on the way down and comes out black rather than red. Doctors call this **melena**.

## Harmless Causes of Black Stool After Drinking

### Pepto-Bismol and other bismuth products

This is by far the most common explanation. Pepto-Bismol, Kaopectate, and many store-brand "stomach relief" liquids and chewables contain **bismuth subsalicylate**. When bismuth meets small amounts of sulfur in your saliva and digestive tract, it forms bismuth sulfide, which is black. The result is black stool and sometimes a black tongue.

The product's own label tells you this can happen and that it's temporary and harmless. It usually shows up within a day of taking it and fades within a couple of days after your last dose.

A few things to know:

- **Pepto-black stool is usually dark gray-black and formed**, not sticky and tarry. It doesn't usually come with the very strong, distinctive smell that digested blood has.
- **It doesn't make you feel unwell.** If you took Pepto and also feel lightheaded or weak, don't assume the Pepto explains everything.
- **Pepto contains a salicylate**, a relative of aspirin. That matters if you drink a lot, because salicylates and alcohol can both irritate the stomach lining. Our guide to [Pepto-Bismol and alcohol](/never-hungover/pepto-bismol-and-alcohol) covers how to use it sensibly after drinking.

### Iron supplements

Iron pills, and multivitamins that contain a lot of iron, commonly turn stool dark green to black. Like bismuth, this is expected and harmless. Iron can also cause constipation or an upset stomach, which a hangover doesn't help. If you started an iron supplement recently, that's a likely explanation.

### Activated charcoal

Some "hangover" and "detox" products contain activated charcoal, and some people take charcoal capsules before or after drinking. Charcoal is black and comes out black. For what it's worth, there's no good evidence that charcoal helps with hangovers. It binds poorly to alcohol, which is absorbed quickly from the stomach and small intestine. It can also interfere with the absorption of medicines you take around the same time.

### Dark foods and drinks

Food and drink rarely produce truly black stool, but they can make it very dark. Common ones include:

- Dark beers and stouts in large amounts
- Red wine in large amounts
- Black licorice (including licorice liqueurs)
- Blueberries, blackberries, and dark grape juice
- Foods with heavy dark food coloring, such as black frosting, dark sandwich cookies, or black-colored burgers and buns
- Squid ink dishes
- Large amounts of dark leafy greens (more often dark green than black)

The key with food is that the color matches what you ate, the stool is otherwise normal, and you feel fine. It should go back to normal within a day or two.

## When Black Stool Means Bleeding

Here's the part to take seriously. Black stool from bleeding happens when blood is lost into the upper digestive tract and travels down through the gut. On the way, stomach acid and enzymes break down the hemoglobin in the blood, which turns it black and gives it a distinct look and smell.

### Alcohol-related causes of upper GI bleeding

Drinking can contribute to bleeding in a few ways. Most of these are more likely with heavy drinking, binges, or combining alcohol with certain painkillers, rather than a couple of drinks with dinner.

- **Gastritis (inflamed stomach lining).** Alcohol, especially in large amounts or strong spirits, irritates and can erode the stomach lining. Mild gastritis is common after a big night and usually heals on its own. More severe erosion can bleed.
- **Peptic ulcers.** Alcohol alone is not the main cause of ulcers. That's usually the bacteria *H. pylori* or regular use of anti-inflammatory painkillers. But alcohol can make an existing ulcer worse, and the combination of alcohol with aspirin, ibuprofen, or naproxen raises the risk of ulcer bleeding.
- **Mallory-Weiss tear.** Repeated, forceful vomiting or retching can tear the lining where the esophagus meets the stomach. It's classically linked to binge drinking followed by hard vomiting. These tears often cause vomiting of bright red blood or streaks, but some blood can be swallowed and come out as dark stool. Many heal on their own, but they need a medical check.
- **Esophageal varices.** In people with advanced liver disease (cirrhosis), blood backs up and swells the veins in the esophagus. These can bleed heavily. This is a medical emergency, and it's a reason anyone with known liver disease should treat black stool as urgent.

### The painkiller factor

The single biggest avoidable risk for a social drinker is reaching for **aspirin, ibuprofen (Advil, Motrin), or naproxen (Aleve)** after drinking. These are called NSAIDs, which stands for non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs. They reduce the stomach's protective mucus layer, and alcohol irritates the same lining. The US Drug Facts labels on these products include a stomach bleeding warning that specifically mentions people who have three or more alcoholic drinks every day.

One or two standard doses with food after a night out is unlikely to cause bleeding in a healthy person. The risk climbs with higher doses, repeated doses over several days, an empty stomach, older age, a history of ulcers, and blood thinners. If you've been taking NSAIDs on top of drinking and now have black stool, mention it to your doctor. Our guides on [ibuprofen and alcohol](/never-hungover/ibuprofen-and-alcohol) and [aspirin and alcohol](/never-hungover/aspirin-and-alcohol) go into the details.

## How to Tell the Difference: Pepto Black vs. Bleeding Black

You can't diagnose yourself from a look in the toilet, but these differences are a useful guide.

| Feature | More likely harmless (Pepto, iron, food) | More likely bleeding (melena) |
|---|---|---|
| Texture | Normal, formed, or a bit loose | Sticky, tar-like, shiny, can smear |
| Smell | Normal stool smell | Unusually strong and foul, different from usual |
| Color | Dark gray-black, black-green, or very dark brown | Jet black, sometimes with a maroon tint |
| Clear cause | You took bismuth, iron, or charcoal, or ate something dark | No obvious explanation |
| How you feel | Fine, or just hungover | Dizzy, weak, faint, pale, short of breath, racing heart |
| Other signs | None | Vomiting blood or "coffee grounds," stomach pain, sweating |
| Timing | Clears within a few days of stopping the cause | Persists or recurs |

A few honest caveats:

- **Pepto can hide a bleed.** If you took Pepto-Bismol and you're also bleeding, the bismuth color can mask what's going on. That's why how you feel matters as much as how the stool looks.
- **Feeling hungover can overlap with early blood loss.** Fatigue, lightheadedness, and a fast heart rate are common the morning after drinking. If those symptoms are getting worse rather than better as the day goes on, or you nearly faint when you stand up, get checked.
- **A doctor can test for blood easily.** A simple stool test for hidden blood, a blood count, and a few questions usually sort it out quickly.

## Bright Red Blood vs. Black Stool: Where the Bleeding Is

If what you saw was red rather than black, the picture changes. The color of blood in stool is a rough clue to where it came from. Blood from high in the gut (the esophagus, stomach, or first part of the small intestine) gets digested on the way down and comes out black. Blood from near the exit arrives fresh and red.

| What you see | What it usually means | How urgent |
|---|---|---|
| Bright red streaks on the stool or toilet paper, or a few drops in the bowl | Bleeding near the anus or rectum, most often a hemorrhoid or a small tear (fissure) | Usually not an emergency. See a doctor if it lasts more than a day or two or keeps coming back |
| Bright red blood mixed through loose stool (bloody diarrhea) | An inflamed colon, from food poisoning, a flare of inflammatory bowel disease, or less often reduced blood flow to the bowel | See a doctor promptly, and the same day with fever, severe belly pain, or signs of dehydration |
| Dark red or maroon stool, or clots | Bleeding higher in the colon, or a fast, heavy bleed from higher up | Get care the same day. Go to the ER if it's heavy or you feel faint |
| Black, sticky, tar-like stool | Digested blood from the upper gut (melena) | Get care the same day. Go to the ER if you're dizzy, weak, or vomiting blood |

### Why drinking can bring on bright red bleeding

The most common source of bright red blood after a night out is a hemorrhoid (a swollen blood vessel near the anus) or a fissure, and alcohol makes both more likely to bleed in two opposite ways. It speeds up the gut and causes loose, frequent stools, which irritate the area (see our guide to [diarrhea after drinking](/never-hungover/diarrhea-after-drinking)). It also dehydrates you, which can leave you with hard stools a day or two later that you strain to pass (see [does alcohol dehydrate you](/never-hungover/does-alcohol-dehydrate-you)). Sitting on the toilet for a long time while you feel rough adds pressure too.

A few caveats keep this from being a simple "red means minor" rule:

- **A very fast bleed from the stomach can come out red.** Red blood with dizziness, fainting, or a racing heart is an emergency, whatever the color.
- **A little blood looks like a lot.** A few drops can turn the toilet water red, so it's hard to judge the amount by eye. Clots or more than a small amount need care the same day.
- **Rule out dye first.** Red sports drinks, fruit punch, grenadine, red gelatin shots, and beets can tint stool red. Dye usually colors the stool evenly and doesn't leave fresh blood on the paper. If you haven't had any of those, treat red as blood until a doctor says otherwise.

If you see a small amount of bright red blood on the paper, you feel well, and you can link it to diarrhea or straining, it's reasonable to drink water, eat fiber, wipe gently, skip ibuprofen-type painkillers, and take a break from alcohol for a day or two while you watch. See a doctor if it doesn't stop, comes back after the next night of drinking, comes with a change in bowel habits, weight loss, or tiredness, or if you're 45 or older. "It's probably a hemorrhoid" is the most common answer, but it's one a doctor should give you.

## Other Stool Colors After Drinking (and What They Mean)

People who search for black stool often notice other colors too. Here's a quick guide.

- **Dark green.** Very common after drinking, especially with diarrhea. Alcohol can speed up how fast food moves through your gut, so bile doesn't have time to break down fully from green to brown. Iron and leafy greens can also cause it. Usually harmless. See our guide to [diarrhea after drinking](/never-hungover/diarrhea-after-drinking) for why alcohol loosens stools.
- **Very dark brown.** Often from dark beer, red wine, or dehydration making stool more concentrated. Usually harmless.
- **Pale, clay, or gray-white.** This can point to a problem with bile flow from the liver or gallbladder, especially with yellow skin or eyes or dark urine. That one needs a doctor.

## Is It the Alcohol or the Hangover Remedies?

This is worth thinking through, because the answer is usually "the remedies."

Alcohol by itself doesn't normally turn stool black. A healthy person who has a few drinks and nothing else should expect, at most, looser or greener stool the next day. When black stool shows up after a night out, ask yourself what else went in:

1. **Did you take Pepto-Bismol, Kaopectate, or a pink stomach-relief product?** That's very likely the answer.
2. **Did you take iron, a multivitamin with iron, or an activated charcoal product?** Also a likely answer.
3. **Did you drink a lot of dark beer or red wine, or eat dark-colored food?** Possible, though it more often makes stool dark brown or green than truly black.
4. **Did you vomit hard and repeatedly?** That raises the chance of a tear and bleeding.
5. **Did you take aspirin, ibuprofen, or naproxen, especially more than one dose or on an empty stomach?** That raises the chance of stomach bleeding.
6. **Do you drink heavily most days, or have known liver disease or a history of ulcers?** Then don't try to explain it away. Get checked.

If the answer to 1, 2, or 3 is yes and you feel fine, waiting a couple of days is reasonable. If the answer to 4, 5, or 6 is yes, or you can't find a harmless explanation, call your doctor.

## How Long Should Black Stool Last?

- **After Pepto-Bismol:** usually gone within a couple of days of your last dose. If it's still black several days after you stopped, call your doctor.
- **After iron supplements:** it will continue as long as you take the iron. That's normal.
- **After activated charcoal:** usually a day or two.
- **After dark food or drink:** usually a day or so, sometimes two.
- **From bleeding:** it won't reliably follow a neat timeline, and it may continue or come back. If there's no harmless cause and it lasts more than a day or two, see a doctor.

## What to Do Right Now

If you've just noticed black stool after drinking, here's a sensible order of steps.

1. **Check how you feel.** Stand up slowly. If you feel faint, your heart is pounding, you're short of breath, or you're pale and clammy, get emergency care now.
2. **Look for vomiting of blood.** Red blood or dark "coffee grounds" material in vomit means go to the emergency room.
3. **Think back over the last 48 hours.** Pepto, iron, charcoal, dark food and drink, painkillers, and how much you drank and vomited.
4. **Stop the likely cause** if it's a remedy you don't need, and stop NSAID painkillers for now. If you need something for a headache, ask a pharmacist what's appropriate for you.
5. **Skip alcohol until it clears.** Give your stomach lining a break, and it also avoids muddying the picture.
6. **Eat bland food and drink water.** Toast, rice, bananas, crackers, and soup are easy on an irritated stomach.
7. **Watch the next few bowel movements.** If they return to normal and you feel fine, it was very likely the remedy or food. If not, call your doctor.
8. **Take a photo if you're unsure.** It sounds awkward, but it can help a doctor or nurse assess what you saw.

## Who Should Be More Careful

Black stool deserves a quicker call to your doctor if you:

- Take **blood thinners** (such as warfarin, apixaban, or rivaroxaban) or daily aspirin
- Regularly take **ibuprofen, naproxen, or other NSAIDs**, including for back or joint pain
- Have had a **stomach ulcer** or GI bleed before
- Have **liver disease**, including fatty liver or cirrhosis, or have been told your liver enzymes are high
- Drink **heavily most days** or binge often
- Are **older**, since the risk of ulcer bleeding rises with age
- Have **anemia**, or have been feeling unusually tired and short of breath for weeks

None of this means you've got a bleed. It just means you have less room to wait and see.

If you notice you need a remedy every time you drink, or your stomach is regularly upset after nights out, that's useful information. Our guides to [stomach pain after drinking](/never-hungover/stomach-pain-after-drinking) and [how alcohol affects your gut](/never-hungover/gut-health-alcohol-microbiome-protection) cover what's going on and how to ease it.

## How to Avoid This Next Time

Most black-stool scares come from the remedy pile, and most stomach bleeding risk comes from heavy drinking and painkillers. A few habits help with both:

- **Eat before and while you drink.** Food in the stomach slows alcohol absorption and cushions the lining. See our guide on [drinking on an empty stomach](/never-hungover/drinking-on-an-empty-stomach).
- **Pace yourself and alternate with water.** Fewer drinks over more time means less irritation and less chance of vomiting.
- **Go easy on straight spirits.** Highly concentrated alcohol is harsher on the stomach lining than drinks that are more diluted.
- **Don't take NSAIDs before bed "just in case."** If you need a painkiller the next morning, eat first and take a single standard dose.
- **Remember what you took.** If you use Pepto, know that black stool is a normal side effect so it doesn't frighten you, but also don't let it stop you noticing if you feel unwell.
- **Don't try to "power through" repeated vomiting.** If you can't keep water down for several hours, or you see blood, get help.

## Can a Supplement Help?

No. No supplement or hangover product protects the stomach lining, prevents bleeding, or changes what black stool means. If you have any of the bleeding signs above, get medical care first. If you take blood thinners or have liver disease, check with your doctor before adding any supplement at all.

## The Bottom Line

- Black stool after drinking is most often caused by **Pepto-Bismol (bismuth), iron, activated charcoal, or dark food and drink**, not the alcohol itself. In those cases it's harmless and clears within a few days.
- **Tarry, sticky, foul-smelling black stool**, especially with dizziness, weakness, a racing heart, or vomiting blood or coffee-ground material, can mean bleeding in the upper digestive tract and needs urgent care.
- Heavy drinking, repeated hard vomiting, NSAID painkillers, blood thinners, ulcers, and liver disease all raise the chance that black stool is blood.
- If you can't find a harmless explanation, or it lasts more than a couple of days after you stop the likely cause, call your doctor. A simple test can tell whether there's blood.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Is black stool after drinking alcohol normal?**

Not always, and you should rule out bleeding first: tarry, sticky, foul-smelling black stool, especially with dizziness or vomiting blood, needs emergency care. The usual explanation is something taken alongside the drinks: Pepto-Bismol (bismuth), iron supplements, activated charcoal, or very dark food and drink. If you took one of those and feel fine, the color should clear within a few days. If there's no clear cause, or the stool is tarry and foul-smelling, get checked.

**Can Pepto-Bismol turn your stool black after drinking?**

Yes. Bismuth in Pepto-Bismol and similar products reacts with small amounts of sulfur in your gut to form a black compound, which turns stool and sometimes the tongue black. The label notes this is temporary and harmless. It usually fades within a couple of days of your last dose. If you also feel dizzy, weak, or faint, don't assume Pepto explains it.

**How can I tell if black stool is blood?**

Stool from bleeding (melena) is usually jet black, sticky and tar-like, shiny, and has an unusually strong, foul smell. It often comes with dizziness, weakness, a racing heart, paleness, or vomiting blood or coffee-ground material. Stool darkened by Pepto, iron, or food is usually formed, smells normal, and you feel fine. You can't be certain by looking, so if you have doubts a doctor can do a quick stool test for blood.

**Can alcohol cause stomach bleeding?**

It can, mostly with heavy drinking. Alcohol irritates and can erode the stomach lining (gastritis), can worsen existing ulcers, and repeated hard vomiting after a binge can tear the lining near the top of the stomach. Combining alcohol with aspirin, ibuprofen, or naproxen raises the risk further. In people with advanced liver disease, swollen veins in the esophagus can bleed heavily, which is an emergency.

**When should I go to the ER for black stool after drinking?**

Go to the emergency room or call 911 if black stool comes with dizziness or fainting, a racing heart, shortness of breath, cold or clammy skin, confusion, or vomiting blood or coffee-ground material. Call your doctor the same day if you can't explain the black stool, it lasts more than two or three days after stopping the likely cause, or you take blood thinners or NSAIDs, have liver disease, or have had an ulcer.

**What does bright red blood in stool after drinking mean?**

Bright red blood on the toilet paper or streaked on the stool usually comes from near the anus, most often a hemorrhoid or a small tear, which alcohol-related diarrhea or straining can irritate. It's usually not an emergency, but see a doctor if it lasts more than a day or two or keeps coming back. A lot of red or maroon blood, clots, or any bleeding with dizziness or a racing heart needs emergency care, because a fast bleed from higher up can also look red.

**How long does black stool last after Pepto-Bismol?**

Usually a day or two after your last dose, sometimes a little longer. If your stool is still black several days after you stopped taking it, or you start feeling unwell, call your doctor.

**Can dark beer or red wine make your poop black?**

Large amounts of dark beer, stout, or red wine can make stool very dark brown or greenish, and occasionally close to black. Truly black, tarry stool is unlikely to be from drinks alone. If the color doesn't match what you had, or doesn't return to normal within a day or two, get it checked.
